hit.title: AgentCore runtime instances are now generally available
hit.body: Today, AWS announces runtime instances, a new feature in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that lets you run agents on your own Amazon EC2 instances without managing infrastructure. AgentCore runtime provides purpose-built infrastructure to deploy and operate AI agents securely at scale. Runtime instances complement the existing microVM-based option in AgentCore runtime and give teams running sustained, resource-intensive, or specialized-hardware agents access to the breadth of EC2 instance types, while AgentCore handles provisioning, patching, scaling, and lifecycle management. Using the AWS Management Console, CLI, SDKs, or APIs, you create a capacity provider that specifies the EC2 instance types your agents need, including GPU-accelerated, memory-optimized, and compute-optimized families, and attach your agents to it. Runtime instances support long-running agent sessions of up to 14 days, while the default serverless, microVM-based runtime is designed for sessions of up to 8 hours that need fast startup . You can choose the right compute for each agent, or run a mix, without changing how you deploy or invoke your agents. You can use runtime instances in the following AWS Regions: US Ea
hit.reason: AgentCore runtime now supports EC2-backed instances with 14-day session limits and specialized hardware, fundamentally expanding its capability profile beyond the existing microVM option and changing deployment recommendations for sustained/resource-intensive agents.

step1.summary: AgentCore runtime now splits into two compute options: default serverless microVM (8h session cap, unchanged) and new EC2-backed "runtime instances" (sessions up to 14 days). The 8h cap is no longer the single session-cap value for AgentCore — it now applies only to the microVM path.
step1.old_value: AgentCore Runtime session cap: 8h (single value, applies to all AgentCore runtime)
step1.new_value: AgentCore Runtime session cap now dimensioned by compute type: microVM (default, serverless) = 8h (unchanged); EC2-backed runtime instances (new, GA) = up to 14 days, using capacity providers with GPU/memory/compute-optimized EC2 instance families
step1.still_true: The 8h session cap remains correct for the default serverless microVM-based AgentCore runtime path.
step1.reasoning: This is a genuine AgentCore feature affecting agentcore.md and design-ref-agentic-to-agentcore.md, which both state '8h' as the single session cap value; now that value only holds for the microVM path while a new EC2-backed path allows 14-day sessions, so the fact's shape gains a new dimension (compute type) rather than simply changing its number. poc-shapes.md's use of 'temporal_worker_poll'/'ecs' etc. is unrelated to AgentCore session caps, so it's a false positive for this specific fact even though it appears in the scan.

affected.after: - Session cap: dimensioned by compute type — microVM (default, serverless) = 8h (unchanged); EC2-backed runtime instances (new, GA) = up to 14 days via capacity providers (GPU/memory/compute-optimized EC2 families)
affected.why: Announcement replaces the single flat 8h cap with a compute-type-dimensioned cap: microVM stays 8h, EC2-backed runtime instances now support up to 14 days.

affected.after: - Session cap: 8h (max 28,800s) — same as AgentCore's default microVM runtime path; AgentCore's new EC2-backed runtime instances now support up to 14 days, so Lambda MicroVMs is shorter than that option

AgentCore now offers a 14-day option via EC2-backed runtime instances, so Lambda MicroVMs is no longer equal to the full range of AgentCore session caps — this comparison needs updating even though it's not a full flip (microVM path is unchanged).

This scoring rule's blanket 'AgentCore has an 8hr session cap' reason is now only true for one compute type and must be updated to avoid disqualifying long-session agents that could use runtime instances.

step2.notes:
[b1] Only hits directly discussing AgentCore's session cap value or judgments/comparisons derived from that cap were treated as affected. Generic mentions of 'AgentCore runtime', 'microVM', or 'Lambda MicroVMs' unrelated to session duration (e.g., SKILL.md triggers, poc-shapes.md artifacts, confirm.md/design.md routing logic, billing notes) are unaffected because they don't state or depend on the specific 8h/session-cap value. The lambda-microvms.md line 17 hit is borderline between value and derived since it repeats the old cap as a comparison basis but its real content is a comparative judgment ('same as...NOT longer') that no longer holds fully true. [b2] All 30 grep hits in this batch are unaffected by the session-cap change. The "[microVM]" hits refer to "Lambda MicroVMs" — a distinct Lambda-based deployment/runtime target used in design/estimate/generate/migration-plan/poc docs for enumerating runtime options (agentcore | lambda_microvms | ecs | eks | lambda | batch | fargate) and cost anchors — this is an unrelated concept from AWS Lambda, not the AgentCore Runtime's microVM-based default execution environment discussed in the announcement. None of these lines state or depend on any session duration/cap value. The "[AgentCore runtime]" hits describe architectural/deployment facts (entrypoint server, container image, POC staging, retarget logic, harness injection) that do not reference or depend on session length/duration at all — they are about routing/POC/deployment mechanics unrelated to the 8h/14-day session cap distinction. Since the change is scoped specifically to session duration limits (agentcore.session_cap), and none of these lines mention session duration, timeouts, or make a duration-dependent recommendation, all are classified unaffected. [b3] Key affected hits: agentcore.json line 8 is a scoring rule that hard-codes the old blanket 8hr cap as disqualifying for AgentCore — this needs to be updated since EC2-backed runtime instances now support up to 14 days, otherwise agents needing long sessions could be wrongly scored against AgentCore. design-ref-agentic-to-agentcore.md line 141 is the clearest 'flipped' case: the recommendation to break tasks into sub-tasks for >8h sessions is a workaround for a limitation that the new EC2-backed runtime instances tier removes. Lines 17 and 130 in the same file state the 8-hour figure as an unqualified fact about AgentCore Runtime generally, which is now incomplete since it's specific to the default microVM path. All lambda_microvms.json and scoring-result.json hits are about a different, unrelated product (Lambda MicroVMs) despite the similar naming, and are unaffected. The poc.md hits reference lambda_microvms infra/deployment mechanics unrelated to the AgentCore session-duration fact. [b4] Batch 4 focuses mainly on clarify-ai.md's task_duration decision table, which is the most directly affected content since it encodes judgments/recommendations keyed to the old flat 8h session cap. Lines 488, 489, and 518 required rewrites: line 489 is a 'flipped' classification because the old recommendation (decompose tasks / use ECS/EKS for >8h tasks) is now reversed — AgentCore Runtime with EC2-backed instances can now handle up to 14-day sessions directly. Lines 488 and 518 are 'derived' since the underlying judgment (recommend AgentCore, or flag session limit issues) needs updated nuance about compute type, but the core recommendation direction doesn't fully reverse. Line 581 is 'derived' since task_duration's role expands to also determine compute type.

All other hits (Harness-specific session limits, monitoring/rollback windows, region tables, pricing, deployment script text, and an unrelated Heroku '14 days' replay window) are unaffected because they either reference a different system (Harness, not AgentCore Runtime), a different kind of duration (monitoring/rollback windows), or no session-cap-specific claim at all. Note that Harness's 8-hour limit (line 17 in design-ref-harness.md) is explicitly a Harness session limit, distinct from AgentCore Runtime's session cap discussed in the announcement, so left unaffected despite the surface-level 8-hour match. [b5] The single grep hit in this batch does not relate to AgentCore Runtime session caps — it appears to be a generic interview question option about a '14 days' timeframe unconnected to compute type or session duration limits. No rewrite needed.
